# 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court Election
## Lead
The 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election refers to the judicial retention election held on November 4, 2025, for three sitting justices of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court: Christine Donohue, Kevin M. Dougherty, and David N. Wecht. Voters were asked to vote “Yes” or “No” on whether each justice should be retained for another ten-year term on the state’s highest court. All three justices won retention by a comfortable margin, each receiving roughly 63% “Yes” votes. The result preserved the court’s existing 5–2 majority of justices elected as Democrats, thwarting an effort by Republican-aligned groups to unseat the justices and alter the court’s ideological balance. The 2025 retention election drew unprecedented attention and campaign spending for a normally low-profile judicial vote, reflecting the high stakes perceived by both major parties.
## Background
Pennsylvania’s constitution requires appellate judges and justices to run in nonpartisan retention elections at the end of each 10-year term, rather than facing challengers in a contested race. Voters simply choose “Yes” (to retain) or “No” (to remove) for each judge on the ballot. If a justice is retained, they earn another ten-year term; if not, the seat becomes vacant. In the event of a vacancy, the governor may appoint a temporary replacement with two-thirds approval of the state Senate, and a partisan election for a full term would be held at the next municipal election (in this case, 2027). Since the modern retention system was adopted in 1968, only one Pennsylvania Supreme Court justice has ever lost a retention vote: Justice Russell Nigro was removed by voters in 2005 amid public anger over a government pay raise scandal. Retention races in Pennsylvania have traditionally attracted little controversy or spending, and judges almost always win re-election by wide margins.
The 2025 retention election was unique because three state Supreme Court justices appeared on the ballot simultaneously – an unusually high number. Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht had all been initially elected to the Supreme Court in 2015 during a rare three-seat contest that flipped the court’s partisan control from Republican to Democratic. Since 2015 the court has had a Democratic-leaning majority (5–2 by 2025), which has handed down significant decisions on politically charged issues such as mail-in voting rules, congressional redistricting, COVID-19 policies, and abortion access. These rulings made the court a focus of partisan interest. Heading into 2025, Republicans saw an opportunity to “break” the Democratic majority by voting “No” on retention and thus opening up seats for potential GOP replacements. If even one justice were not retained, a statewide election for that seat would occur in 2027, giving Republicans a chance to win a new seat on the court. Had all three been removed, the court could have been left evenly split between Democratic and Republican-aligned justices in the interim, a scenario observers warned would risk deadlocks on important cases during the 2026–2028 election cycle. This high-stakes context set the stage for an unusually intense retention campaign.
## Campaign
Although judicial retention elections in Pennsylvania are officially nonpartisan and typically low-key, the 2025 Supreme Court retention race became highly politicized and broke spending records. Both major parties and outside interest groups treated it as a proxy battle for control of the court. Republican and conservative organizations launched a coordinated “vote no” campaign aimed at removing the three justices. Their messaging highlighted controversial court decisions and portrayed the retention vote as a rare chance to impose accountability. For example, ads funded by GOP-aligned groups and wealthy donors (such as billionaire Jeffrey Yass) attacked the justices for “radical” liberal rulings: they noted the court’s role in overturning Bill Cosby’s sexual assault conviction on due-process grounds and in rejecting a Republican-favored congressional district map as unconstitutional. Some anti-retention mailers urged voters to “Term Limit the Court”, framing a “No” vote as a way to oust longtime incumbents and reset the judiciary. This rhetoric tapped into popular sentiment for term limits and dissatisfaction with government, according to political analysts.
On the other side, Democratic officials, labor unions, and progressive groups mobilized a “vote yes” effort to defend the justices. Supporters argued that retaining Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht would preserve an independent judiciary and protect civil rights. Democratic messaging emphasized issues like abortion rights, voting rights, and fair elections, warning that conservative activists were trying to “buy” the court and roll back protections. Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and national Democratic figures openly campaigned for a “Yes” vote on retention. Even former President Barack Obama weighed in with support for retaining the justices, while former President Donald Trump urged Pennsylvania voters to reject them. This unusually high-profile involvement underscored the national significance that both sides attached to the normally obscure retention contests.
Campaign spending shattered previous records for judicial retention elections in the state. In past cycles, retention races saw at most a few hundred thousand dollars in spending, but in 2025 the spending ran into the tens of millions. By Election Day, over $16 million had been poured into advertising and voter outreach for the Supreme Court retention votes, predominantly by pro-retention (Democratic) groups. The Democratic side outspent the anti-retention campaign roughly 4-to-1, according to news reports, funding television ads, mailers, and get-out-the-vote operations statewide. Republican committees (such as the Republican State Leadership Committee) and allied PACs still invested significant resources in digital ads and mail, but were ultimately outmatched in spending and ground game. All three justices were also endorsed by the Pennsylvania Bar Association, which recommended voters retain them and described each as fair and qualified. The convergence of national partisan attention, large donations from special interests, and active campaigning by the judges themselves made this retention election “historic” in its level of politicization. One local media outlet noted that 2025’s battle “dealt a blow to the idea that retention votes are nonpartisan affairs,” as it came to resemble a typical partisan contest in all but name.
## Results
The retention election was held on November 4, 2025, alongside Pennsylvania’s municipal general elections. Turnout was higher than usual for a judicial off-year election, reflecting the intense interest. On election night, the Associated Press called the Supreme Court retention races in favor of all three justices by around 10 p.m., less than two hours after polls closed. Unofficial returns showed a clear mandate to retain each justice. Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht each received approximately 63–64% “Yes” votes to 36–37% “No” votes statewide, margins of roughly 26–28 percentage points in favor of retention. These margins are in line with the traditionally strong public support that incumbent judges enjoy in retention elections. All three justices were thus elected to serve additional ten-year terms on the Supreme Court, which will extend into the mid-2030s.
The outcome was hailed by Democrats as a major victory for judicial independence. Gov. Josh Shapiro lauded the voters for “sending a resounding message” in favor of retaining the justices, saying they would continue to uphold the rule of law and protect constitutional rights on the court. Democratic Party leaders noted that the result maintains the court’s 5–2 liberal majority through upcoming election cycles. With all three justices remaining in office, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s ideological balance was unchanged, preventing any immediate shift on hot-button issues such as election oversight and redistricting. Voters essentially rejected the Republican effort to “flip” the court, opting for stability on the bench.
On the other hand, conservatives expressed disappointment at failing to unseat any justice. Some Republican strategists argued that the politicization of judicial races would continue and vowed to contest the open seat that is expected in 2027. Justice Christine Donohue will reach Pennsylvania’s mandatory judicial retirement age of 75 in 2027, which will require her to leave the court before her new term is complete. That impending vacancy is slated to be filled by a partisan election in November 2027, offering the GOP another chance to gain a seat on the court. Until then, the Supreme Court’s composition will remain the same. The avoidance of any immediate vacancies also spared Pennsylvania’s judicial system from potential disruption. Had one or more justices been removed, their seats would have stood vacant until the 2027 election (barring a difficult interim appointment agreement), possibly leading to deadlocked 3–3 decisions on high-profile cases. By winning retention, the three justices ensured continuity and a full complement of seven justices on the bench.
The 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election is likely to be remembered for its partisan overtones and record spending. It demonstrated that even nominally noncompetitive judicial elections can become major political battlegrounds when control of a high court is at stake. In the end, Pennsylvania voters decisively chose to retain all the justices, reaffirming the historical trend that sitting judges are rarely removed at the ballot box. The court’s liberal majority was preserved heading into the 2026–2028 period, and any further shifts will depend on future judicial elections and retirements. As only the second statewide retention election in Pennsylvania to attract such intense scrutiny (after 2005’s Nigro vote), the 2025 contest may influence how political parties approach judicial retention races in the future.

### Follow WHYY News' election coverage

*   **🖥️** [**WHYY.org**](https://whyy.org/elections-2025/): Read the latest coverage and track race results
*   **📱** [**WHYY App**](https://whyy.org/whyy-listen-app/): Read the latest election updates and stream WHYY-FM

Pennsylvania residents had the opportunity to vote in local and statewide judicial elections, from municipal judges all the way up to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. While such off-year elections have traditionally been low-key, this year proved to be different with millions of dollars going into the Supreme Court retention race which, in turn, brought an unusual level of attention to the other judicial races, as well.

Here are the results.

Pennsylvania voters answered “yes” to the retention of Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin M. Dougherty and David N. Wecht on the state’s highest court, preserving the 5-2 Democratic-elected majority on the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania.

The results mark a decisive moment for the judicial branch in the commonwealth, [following a year of unprecedented attention](https://whyy.org/articles/pennsylvania-election-2025-supreme-court-retention-dnc/) — and expenditures — on what has traditionally been a low-profile process of judicial retention.

*   [WHYY thanks our sponsors — become a WHYY sponsor](https://whyy.org/corporate-underwriting/ "WHYY thanks our sponsors — become a WHYY sponsor")

By giving each justice another 10-year term on the bench, voters effectively rejected efforts to alter the ideological composition of the court. The Democratic-elected majority remains intact, limiting the prospect of a partisan shift in key decisions in years to come.

Although retention elections in Pennsylvania are nonpartisan in name — voters mark “yes” or “no” without party affiliation — this year’s fight took on a strikingly partisan cast. The three justices had originally been elected as Democrats in 2015 and have since issued rulings on major — albeit divisive — issues, including abortion access, voting rules, electoral maps and COVID restrictions.

Republicans and right-wing activists blasted those decisions and [sought to take advantage of the rare opportunity to change the overall direction of the court](https://whyy.org/articles/pennsylvania-gop-supreme-court-republicans-election/) by mounting an unprecedented effort to get Wecht, Donohue and Dougherty removed from their benches, which also prompted Democrats to get more involved than in the past.

The scale of campaign spending also soared, underscoring how state courts are increasingly battlegrounds for broader political disputes.

“I got mailers every other day in my mailbox and I saw quite a few ads on TV,” South Philly resident Deborah Dalton said just after she voted.

However, she told WHYY News that the current politics in Washington, D.C., led her to vote to retain all three justices.

“We have enough crap going on every other day,” she said. “You don’t know what’s going on on that national level. I want some consistency here in Philadelphia.”

Prior to the vote, analysts also warned that the court could face a 2-2 partisan deadlock if the three justices failed to win retention and if the governor and Legislature were unable to agree on interim appointments. With the retention secured, that scenario has been avoided, at least for the foreseeable future.

Only two of the three justices are guaranteed to serve another 10-year term, however, as Donohue is due for mandatory retirement in two years when she will reach the age of 75, which will prompt another election.

Commonwealth Court
------------------

In the race to fill one open seat on the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania, voters selected Judge Stella Tsai, a Democrat and longtime member of the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas. Her win preserves a path for Democrats to maintain influence on one of the state’s two intermediate appellate courts.

The Commonwealth Court handles appeals and original jurisdiction cases involving state and local governments, regulatory agencies and election matters, making it a consequential institution for how governance and public-policy disputes are resolved in the commonwealth.

Tsai, born in Harrisburg to immigrant parents from Taiwan, graduated from the University of Pennsylvania and Penn Law, and has served as a judge of the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas since 2016. She told WHYY News before the election that her background helped mold her desire to become a lawyer and then a judge.

“As a child of immigrants who came from a country that was ruled by a pretty repressive regime that imposed martial law in 1997, I understood the importance of democracy at an early age,” she said. “And because of that, a lot of my life has been devoted to the issue of voting rights and free and fair elections and making sure that people have the opportunity to participate in this democracy.”

Voters also retained Judge Michael Wojcik, a Democrat who has served on the Commonwealth Court since 2016 and will now serve another 10-year term. Despite their wins, judges elected as Republicans will continue to hold a majority on the court, now 5 to 4.

*   [WHYY thanks our sponsors — become a WHYY sponsor](https://whyy.org/corporate-underwriting/ "WHYY thanks our sponsors — become a WHYY sponsor")

Superior Court
--------------

Democratic Judge Brandon P. Neuman secured victory to fill the open 10-year term on the Superior Court of Pennsylvania. His win marks a modest but meaningful shift in the 15-member appellate bench, which plays a key role in civil, criminal and family law appeals across the commonwealth.

The seat became vacant after former Judge Daniel D. McCaffery ascended to the state Supreme Court in 2023. In the general election, Neuman faced Republican nominee Maria Battista and Liberal Party candidate Daniel Wassmer.

Democrat Judge Alice Beck DuBow also secured a new 10-year term in a separate retention vote.

The Superior Court hears most appeals from the 67 county courts, setting the tone for how law is applied across the state. Neuman’s victory strengthens the Democratic presence on the court, which currently includes eight judges originally elected as Democrats and six originally elected as Republicans. With this win, the partisan balance tilts further in the Democratic direction — a development likely to resonate in cases involving election law and criminal justice reform.

Philadelphia judges
-------------------

Philadelphia voters completed what had been a largely uncontested judicial cycle: 11 open seats on the Court of Common Pleas and four open seats on the Philadelphia Municipal Court were filled, and all candidates on the Democratic slate prevailed. The outcome affirms the city’s one-party dominance of the bench and underscores how judicial elections in the city continue to be shaped by internal Democratic Party processes rather than competitive partisan battles.

City voters were asked to select 11 new judges to the Court of Common Pleas to fill an equal number of open seats, alongside 13 sitting judges standing for retention. All 11 candidates running for the open seats were Democrats, and each carried the endorsements of the local Democratic Party and the Philadelphia Bar Association, per the voter guide. The slate included  Larry Farnese, Kia Ghee, Leon A. King II, Will Braveman, Brian Kisielewski, Irina Ehrlich, Anthony Stefanski, Deborah Watson‑Stokes, Sarah Jones, Joseph J. Russo and Jennifer A. Santiago.

On the Municipal Court side, the four open seats were won by the only four candidates, Democrats Amanda Davidson, Michael Parkinson, Sherrie Cohen and Cortez Patton.

All of the judges running for reelection were also retained.

Three state Supreme Court justices were elected to second terms Tuesday, despite efforts by conservative groups to persuade voters to oust them, according to unofficial election results.

Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty and David Wecht, first elected as Democrats in 2015, will continue serving on the commonwealth’s highest court, which hears appeals in cases ranging from capital murder cases to congressional redistricting.

Their retention to 10-year terms maintains the court’s 5-2 Democratic majority, although Donohue, 72, will be able to serve only three years before reaching the mandatory retirement age for state judges.

Democratic leaders called the results a victory for judicial independence and a further repudiation of efforts by billionaire political donors to buy court seats.

[![Image 1: Election signs posted in Harrisburg on Nov. 4, 2025. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)](https://penncapital-star.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/judicial-retention-2025-1024x768.jpeg)](https://penncapital-star.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/judicial-retention-2025-scaled.jpeg)

Election signs posted in Harrisburg on Nov. 4, 2025. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)

“Tonight, folks across our commonwealth sent a resounding message by voting to retain all three Supreme Court justices who will continue to defend the rule of law, safeguard our elections, and protect our constitutional rights,” Gov. Josh Shapiro said. “Here in the birthplace of democracy, the good people of Pennsylvania will always stand for freedom.”

Democratic National Committee Chairperson Ken Martin, who campaigned across the state for the justices, said the election was a major win for fair elections, reproductive rights, voting rights, and democracy.

“Tonight, Pennsylvania delivered a message on behalf of the entire country: No matter how rich you are, and no matter how much power you think you might have, our courts are not for sale,” Martin said.

With about half of the vote counted, the votes for each justice stood at about 63% to 37% in favor of retention. Retention vote margins are historically in the range of 60% to 75%.

In other statewide judicial elections, Democrat Brandon Neuman led Republican Maria Batista 56% to 41% in the race for a Superior Court seat and Democrat Stella Tsai led Republican Matt Wolford 57% to 43%. Superior Court Judge Alice Beck Debow and Commonwealth Court Judge Michael Wojcik each held leads in favor of retention.

Since 1968, Pennsylvania has used a system of electing judges initially in contested partisan races and requiring them to stand for retention for subsequent terms. In a retention race, judges face no opponents and voters are asked to decide whether the judge should be retained for another 10-year term.

The retention election for three members of the court created an opening for Republicans to break up the Democratic majority. A non-retention vote for any of the three would have triggered a contested election in 2027.

Subscribe to the Pennsylvania Capital-Star's Morning Guide now.](https://penncapital-star.com/subscribe)Groups associated with billionaire donor Jeffrey Yass launched a campaign late last summer to mobilize voters to “term-limit the Pa. Supreme Court” and to associate Donohue, Dougherty and Wecht with unpopular decisions, such as overturning comedian Bill Cosby’s 2018 aggravated indecent assault conviction.

Another ad said the court was responsible for redrawing congressional districts to help Democrats, while showing a gerrymandered map favored by Republicans that it had actually rejected as unconstitutional.

It’s unclear, until the final campaign finance reports are filed, how much outside groups spent, but the justices and committees supporting them raised at least $14 million.

Nydea Graves, lead democracy coordinator of One Pennsylvania, which promotes progressive, multiracial working class political power, said the vote was a rejection of Yass and the MAGA agenda.

“Voters understood that Pennsylvania needs a court that holds true to the constitution’s promise of equal treatment for all of us. From voting rights to education equity to healthcare to workers’ rights, Pennsylvanians expect the law to be applied fairly, not just in favor of a privileged few,” Graves said.

Donohue, Dougherty and Wecht were originally elected in an unprecedented three-way race. It stemmed from the scandal-driven resignations of two justices and the mandatory retirement of former Chief Justice Ron Castille.

Justice [Joan Orie Melvin resigned](https://www.inquirer.com/philly/news/politics/state/20130325_Convicted__Orie_Melvin_resigns_from_Supreme_Court.html) in 2013 after she was convicted of using her judicial staff and her sister’s state Senate staff to do campaign work. Justice Seamus McCaffery [resigned in 2014](https://www.mcall.com/2014/10/27/seamus-mccaffery-retires-amid-porn-email-scandal/) after it was revealed he sent pornographic emails to an agent in the attorney general’s office as former Attorney General Kathleen Kane’s office investigated her predecessor’s handling of the Jerry Sandusky child sexual abuse case.

Only once, in 2005, has a Supreme Court justice not been retained, when Justice Russell Nigro was voted off the bench in the backlash from a middle-of-the-night vote by state lawmakers to give themselves and judges a pay raise.

HARRISBURG — Pennsylvanians have voted to retain three Democratic state Supreme Court justices, granting them additional terms on the bench after an unusually contentious, multimillion-dollar election.

Republicans and their allies had hoped to defeat the justices and put their seats on the 2027 ballot, opening a path to flip the court. The Democratic majority has handed down critical rulings over the past decade, upholding mail voting and throwing out a congressional map that it found unfairly benefited the GOP.

Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht were on the ballot Tuesday. They were first elected in 2015 in a sweep that flipped the court from Republican to Democratic control.

The Associated Press called all three races at 9:53 p.m. Unofficial results show their margins are all around 27 points.

Superior Court Judge Alice Dubow and Commonwealth Court Judge Michael Wojcik also won their retention races on Tuesday. The Associated Press called those races shortly after 10 p.m.

Retention elections are typically low-interest, low-spending races that favor incumbents. [Only one statewide judge has lost](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/judicial-retention-supreme-court-2025-guide-elections/) their retention election since 1968, when the state constitution was last updated.

These elections provide justices with another 10 years on the bench. However, Donohue will hit the state’s mandatory retirement age of 75 in two years. That means there will be an open, partisan election to fill the vacancy in 2027. (Chief Justice Debra Todd, a Democrat, and Justice Sallie Mundy, a Republican, will be up for retention that year.)

The last state Supreme Court retention elections were held in 2017, with Todd and Thomas Saylor, a Republican who has since retired, on the ballot. Spending on those races — from [the](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20170045) [candidates](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20170017) as well as from special interests via independent expenditures — was relatively low, totaling about $850,000.

Spending this year has well exceeded that total.

Campaign finance records show nearly $3.3 million has been spent by [Dougherty](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20240446) or on his behalf through in-kind donations of goods or services like mailers through Oct. 20. That total is more than $2 million for [Wecht](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20140414) and $1.8 million for [Donohue](https://www.campaignfinanceonline.pa.gov/pages/CFAnnualTotals.aspx?Filer=20250024).

In addition, [a wide range of special interest groups](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-race-spending-independent-expenditures-elections/) — including [Planned Parenthood’s super PAC](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/retention-election-abortion-advertising-supreme-court-pennsylvania-elections/), [Democratic](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/supreme-court-pennsylvania-campaign-finance-november-election-aclu-democratic-yass-elections/) and [Republican](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election/) committees that receive national money, and a [trio of groups](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-race-spending-independent-expenditures-elections/) tied to the state’s richest man, Jeffrey Yass — have spent at least $9.8 million as of Tuesday evening.

Anti-retention groups urged voters to “term limit the court” and “defend our democracy,” and highlighted high-profile decisions, including a ruling to overturn the conviction of comedian Bill Cosby [on a technicality](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/bill-cosby-be-released-after-sexual-assault-conviction-overturned-pennsylvania-n1272748). A Yass-connected group sent out a [mailer](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-misleading-redistricting-claims-elections/) that accused the court of gerrymandering the state’s congressional map “to help Democrats win,” while highlighting a GOP-drawn map thrown out for unfairly benefiting Republicans.

Groups supporting the justices said that the state Supreme Court would defend [reproductive health care](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/10/retention-election-abortion-advertising-supreme-court-pennsylvania-elections/) in the state, and [argued in ads](https://adstransparency.google.com/advertiser/AR14015309208400953345/creative/CR10108323711456116737?region=US&topic=political&start-date=2025-01-01&end-date=2025-10-17) that “billionaires” are “trying to buy our independent and fair courts.”

All three justices were [recommended by the Pennsylvania Bar Association](https://www.pabar.org/site/For-Lawyers/Committees-Commissions/Judicial-Evaluation/Resources/JEC-Ratings/2025/Supreme-Court), which called them “fair,” “open to consideration of differing perspectives,” and “logical.”

Donohue worked as a civil trial lawyer and commercial litigator before being elected to the Superior Court of Pennsylvania in 2007. The Superior is one of two intermediate appellate courts in the state and largely focuses on criminal, family, and civil cases that are appealed up from the county Courts of Common Pleas.

Since her election to the state Supreme Court in 2015, Donohue has been the primary author on a number of high-profile decisions, including one in [2022](https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/2022/14-15-17-18-amp-19-map-2022.html) that upheld Pennsylvania’s no-excuse mail voting law, Act 77.

Dougherty began his career as an assistant district attorney in Philadelphia, then worked in private practice before he was appointed to the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas in 2001. He stayed in that position until his election to the state Supreme Court.

During this retention race, [he has highlighted](https://retaindougherty.com/) his work on a “statewide behavioral health initiative” that involved the establishment, last year, of an Office of Behavioral Health within the courts, and another program that created sensory-friendly courtrooms to accommodate people on the autism spectrum.

Dougherty also has notable family ties. His brother, John Dougherty, was the head of Local 98 of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers for decades before he was sentenced to six years in prison for bribing a city council member and embezzlement. His son, Sean Dougherty, is a member of the state House, serving northeast Philadelphia.

Wecht served as register of wills and clerk of the Orphans Court of Allegheny County before being elected to the county’s Court of Common Pleas. He was then elected to the Superior Court in 2011 before his election to the Supreme Court.

Among the opinions Wecht has written as a Supreme Court justice were [a contentious 2020 ruling](https://www.ballardspahr.com/-/jssmedia/files/alerts/wecht---majority.pdf?rev=a4a7bb8419dc42e990ee0a1ff514f312&hash=5901F14E2B68ED01675A029F4ACDEA40) upholding Gov. Tom Wolf’s pandemic powers, in which he argued that the “Pennsylvania Constitution does not empower the legislature to act unilaterally to suspend” [the state’s disaster law](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2020/07/pennsylvania-coronavirus-disaster-declaration-supreme-court-ruling/), from which Wolf had claimed his authority.

All three Pennsylvania Supreme Court justices on Tuesday’s ballot for retention will remain on the bench, following an unprecedented and closely watched retention election that eclipsed previous spending records as [Democrats](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/democratic-party) sought to protect the liberal judges.

Pennsylvania’s highest court will maintain its liberal majority for at least the next two years, retaining Justices [Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/a/philadelphia-pennsylvania-2025-election-voters-guide-candidates-ballot-20251014.html) through the 2026 midterms and ahead of the 2028 presidential election. During that time, the court will hear cases that affect the daily lives of Pennsylvania residents, on abortion access, voter access, mail voting law, and more. The Associated Press called the race at 9:53 p.m. Tuesday, less than two hours after polls closed.

The stakes of Tuesday’s judicial retention election were set up a decade ago by a convergence of factors. The three justices up for retention — [Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/a/philadelphia-pennsylvania-2025-election-voters-guide-candidates-ballot-20251014.html) — were each elected as Democrats in 2015 during a rare and transitional period for the court when Democrats took a majority. The 2015 election was the first time three seats were open at one time, in part due to resignations of disgraced former justices. Since then, [Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht have played decisive roles](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-cases-justices-retention-election-20251015.html) on the 5-2 liberal majority of Pennsylvania’s highest court.

The retention race — usually a sleepy, off-year affair — this year topped $16 million in ad buys and mailers, [mostly from Democrats or aligned groups,](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/supreme-court-retention-race-pennsylvania-campaign-funding-20251102.html "https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/supreme-court-retention-race-pennsylvania-campaign-funding-20251102.html") to try to draw voters to the polls to protect the liberal majority they view as the last backstop to protect Pennsylvanians’ rights during an overreaching Trump administration. [Republicans](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/republican-party), meanwhile, saw the high-stakes race as what they called a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” to oust three liberal state Supreme Court justices in one election.

Around 10 p.m. on Tuesday, Dougherty, flanked by beaming family members and Philadelphia Democratic City Committee chair Bob Brady, addressed his supporters.

“I don’t know if you’ve heard, but we won,” he told the roaring room, referring to his fresh 10-year term.

Judicial retention elections in Pennsylvania [traditionally attract little attention and little money](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-election-20250511.html). But Republicans viewed this year as an opportunity to overhaul the court, which has become an even more critical battleground under President [Donald Trump](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/donald-trump) as state-level courts hold sway over everything from [abortion rights](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/supreme-court-pennsylvania-retain-justices-josh-shapiro-20251009.html) to [congressional redistricting](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-redistricting-20250916.html).

Only one justice has lost retention since 1968, when the current system was implemented. That justice, Russell Nigro, was ousted in 2005, unrelated to his rulings on the court but reflecting a larger referendum on Pennsylvania state government at the time.

While this year’s retention election was nonpartisan, [Democratic groups and donors outspent Republicans 4-1](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/supreme-court-retention-race-pennsylvania-campaign-funding-20251102.html "https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/supreme-court-retention-race-pennsylvania-campaign-funding-20251102.html"), shelling out more than $13 million on ads reserved through Election Day to retain the three justices on the liberal-majority bench.

Throughout their retention campaigns, Dougherty, Wecht, and Donohue all protested the politicization of what was intended to be a nonpartisan “check” on whether they have upheld their oaths of office. Still, they appeared at fundraisers and in commercials and knocked on doors to ensure they kept their jobs.

Those efforts resonated in South Philly, said Democratic ward leader Michael Sullivan. Turnout in his division was “extremely high,” with voters driven to the polls by the retention election.

The Republican push to “vote no” awoke voters, Sullivan said.

“Democrats countered that with TV advertisements and committee people got out, knocked doors, and got energized over it,” Sullivan added.

### ‘Democratic convictions are at stake’

The Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s decisions have had widespread influence on the lives of the state’s residents, including rulings on [whose mail ballots should be counted](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/pennsylvania-mail-voting-law-act-77-mclinko-20220802.html) under the law, [whether cities can set their own gun laws](https://www.inquirer.com/crime/pa-supreme-court-reject-philly-gun-laws-20241120.html), and shoring up the state’s [constitutional rights for gender equality](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-vote-2025-20251019.html).

Some of those decisions fueled [Republican groups’ attempts to oust the three justices](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-election-20250511.html "https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-election-20250511.html") and reshape the court ahead of the 2028 presidential election. GOP activists, some of whom are still angry with the court for its rulings on business closures and mail ballots during the COVID-19 pandemic, emphasized the three justices’ roles in those decisions as proof they needed to be booted from the bench, even if their seats could remain empty until 2027.

The GOP messaging got through to many Republican voters ahead of Tuesday’s election, with several voters citing their general discontent with the liberal court’s decisions over the last few years.

Nick Touni, 42, of [Ridley Park](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/ridley-park), said he took his local Republican Party’s recommendation and voted against retaining the three justices.

“Change, I think, is necessary,” Touni added.

During the closely watched campaign, some GOP groups used language often used by Democrats to misrepresent or confuse independent voters and registered Democrats to encourage them to vote “no” in the low-information, off-year election. However, in light of the decisive vote in favor of retaining the justices, the efforts did not appear to be successful.

In Mount Airy, Marlon Reid, 45, voted to retain the judges, saying he had already seen negative impacts [after SNAP benefits were halted](https://www.inquirer.com/news/snap-benefits-november-update-shutdown-20251103.html "https://www.inquirer.com/news/snap-benefits-november-update-shutdown-20251103.html") at the beginning of the month due to the federal government shutdown. Reid, a financial counselor for HIV-positive women in Philadelphia, acknowledged that the three justices have little say over what happens at a federal level, but believed it was critical to retain them.

“Keeping the people that we have at the state judicial level feels like our only chance with everything that is going on,” Reid said.

Some voters said they headed to the polls Tuesday due to the issues likely to come before the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, such as [voting rights](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-redistricting-20250916.html "https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-redistricting-20250916.html") or [abortion access](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/supreme-court-pennsylvania-retain-justices-josh-shapiro-20251009.html "https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/supreme-court-pennsylvania-retain-justices-josh-shapiro-20251009.html").

Winifred Gilbert, 78, of Chester, had an abortion when she was a teenager. Ever since then, she said, she has wanted to ensure other women have the same access.

“To think that my granddaughter might have less \[reproductive\] rights, that kills me,” said Maggie Stoeffel, 66, holding back tears outside her [Chestnut Hill](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/chestnut-hill) polling place. “Before, you didn’t even think about the judge’s party, but so much of our democratic convictions are at stake that it’s important to try and hold onto what we can.”

### National attention

The election saw national attention, and [Trump weighed in on the race](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/five-things-supreme-court-retention-election-20251103.html "https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/five-things-supreme-court-retention-election-20251103.html") at the 11th hour, encouraging Pennsylvania voters to vote “no” to keep the justices from serving another term and “bring back the Rule of Law.” He mentioned each justice by name and blamed them for their role in a 2018 redistricting case that he said on Truth Social on Sunday night led to his impeachment by the U.S. House. He also criticized the justices for their roles in mail ballot rulings and COVID-19-related closures in 2020.

“It is time for Justice,” Trump wrote. “Vote ‘NO, NO, NO’ on retention of these woke Judges.”

Democratic heavyweights, [from former President Barack Obama](https://x.com/BarackObama/status/1983634154521526446 "https://x.com/BarackObama/status/1983634154521526446") to Gov. [Josh Shapiro](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/josh-shapiro), all emphasized the importance of the election and asked voters to vote “yes” for the judges’ retention.

Shapiro celebrated their retention as a “resounding message by voters,” he said in a statement.

All three of the justices retained Tuesday have often sided with the liberal court majority’s rulings, though the justices frequently write individual dissenting opinions that represent where they disagree with a final opinion. Each of the justices was recommended for retention by the Pennsylvania Bar Association and had broad support from labor unions, Pennsylvania’s legal community, and out-of-state Democrats.

Dougherty — whose election to the court in 2015 was buoyed by the financial backing of his brother, convicted former labor leader [John Dougherty](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/john-dougherty) — [faced attacks from some GOP influencers throughout the retention election](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/kevin-dougherty-supreme-court-pa-retention-johnny-doc-20251024.html "https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/kevin-dougherty-supreme-court-pa-retention-johnny-doc-20251024.html") for his relation to his brother, as well as accusations from prosecutors during his brother’s federal trials that he accepted free services or goods paid for by embezzled union funds. Kevin Dougherty has maintained he never knowingly accepted gifts from his brother using misused union funds.

In a speech at the Sheet Metal Workers International building in [South Philadelphia](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/south-philly), Dougherty thanked Shapiro and Philadelphia Mayor [Cherelle L. Parker](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/cherelle-parker) for their support. But his biggest thank-you went to the labor unions that supported his retention.

“My biggest shout-out and my biggest heartfelt thanks goes to organized labor. My labor friends across the commonwealth, this victory is yours, as well as the people of Pennsylvania,” Dougherty said.

Since his election to the court, Dougherty, 63, has led an initiative on autism in courts and is now leading a statewide behavioral health initiative to better interact with people with mental health or substance-use disorders. He led Philadelphia’s Family Court for more than a decade before his election to the state Supreme Court in 2015.

Dougherty remarked in his speech Tuesday night he is looking forward to returning his focus to this work now that the retention election is over.

Some voters in the Philadelphia region said they split their retention votes to support Dougherty, a Philadelphia native, while rejecting the two other justices, who live in Pittsburgh.

Wecht, 63, and Donohue, 72, previously served on the state Superior Court, which is known as one of the busiest appeals courts in the country for its handling of most criminal appeals.

Though she was retained, Donohue will not be able to fulfill another full 10-year term. She will be required by the state constitution to leave the bench at the end of 2027 when she turns 75. The next retention elections will take place in 2027, when two justices — a liberal and a conservative — are up for retention.

_Staff writers Nate File, Michelle Myers, and Fallon Roth contributed to this article._

A national Democratic group is getting involved in the Pa. Supreme Court retention elections
============================================================================================

Republicans in November are trying to break Democrats’ 5-2 majority on Pennsylvania's high court, which plays a critical role in redistricting.

![Image 1: Democratic Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justices David Wecht, Christine Donohue, and Kevin Dougherty face retention elections this year.](https://www.inquirer.com/resizer/v2/MACCEIF6F5FFFLEXMHTUXVHUWA.jpg?auth=f612c47053ce1ae37ee31ff45eb830ac628ec1cef487a0ac092391a5d49545fe&width=760&height=507&smart=true)

Democratic Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justices David Wecht, Christine Donohue, and Kevin Dougherty face retention elections this year.Read moreMonica Herndon / Staff Photographer

by [Sean Collins Walsh](https://www.inquirer.com/author/walsh_sean/)

Published Sept. 15, 2025, 5:00 a.m. ET

A national Democratic group that works on state legislative races is making a “six-figure investment” in this year’s Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention elections, the latest sign that the usually sleepy off-year judicial contests are [taking on broader significance](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-election-20250511.html "https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-election-20250511.html").

The Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee will send the money to Pennsylvanians for Judicial Fairness, a group working to reelect Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht, the three incumbent Democratic justices on the ballot this year, DLCC spokesperson Samantha Paisley said.

Advertisement

**» READ MORE: [Republicans are attempting to boot three Democratic justices from the Pa. Supreme Court — and for the first time, Dems are worried](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-election-20250511.html)**

In an interview Friday, Paisley declined to say how much money the DLCC was spending.

DLCC president Heather Williams said the group is “clear-eyed on the major implications that these Pennsylvania state Supreme Court races will have on Democratic legislators’ ability to deliver on their agenda in Harrisburg, as well as the redistricting process at the end of this decade.”

The group’s pledge follows a cash infusion from the national Republican State Leadership Committee for digital ads urging Meta and Google users to “vote no” in the Nov. 4 election, [Spotlight PA reported](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election/ "https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election/").

A fuller financial picture of the race may begin to emerge later this month, when campaign finance reports become available.

Every 10 years, sitting Supreme Court justices face retention elections, in which voters face yes-or-no choices on whether to reelect the justices, rather than a choice between candidates.

If the justices fail to win retention, Democratic Gov. [Josh Shapiro](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/josh-shapiro) could appoint replacements — subject to confirmation in the GOP-controlled state Senate — who would serve until the seats are filled in open elections in 2027. That would allow the newly elected justices to be in place for the next presidential election in 2028 and the redistricting cycle following the 2030 census.

Judicial retention elections rarely draw significant attention. But this year’s races have drawn national interest as [Republicans](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/republican-party) seek to break [Democrats](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/democratic-party)’ 5-2 majority on the state’s high court, which plays a critical role in adjudicating conflicts over election administration.

”Extremist Republicans have made it crystal clear they are willing to weaponize the judiciary to keep themselves in power, and we will not stand back and allow them to undermine the voices of the voters in Pennsylvania or anywhere else,“ Williams said in a statement.

Meanwhile, state Republican Party spokesperson [James Markley said recently](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/dougherty-donohue-wecht-supreme-court-retention-20250908.html "https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/dougherty-donohue-wecht-supreme-court-retention-20250908.html") that the incumbent justices have “spent their careers as partisan Democrats, making blatantly political rulings.”

“Voters deserve better,” Markley said. “It’s time to bring fairness and integrity back to the highest court in our Commonwealth.”

_Staff writer Gillian McGoldrick contributed to this article._

Dougherty](https://ballotpedia.org/Kevin_M._Dougherty "Kevin M. Dougherty") (D), and [David N. Wecht](https://ballotpedia.org/David_N._Wecht "David N. Wecht") (D) — were [retained](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention "Retention") in three elections held on November 4, 2025. _WHYY_'s Carmen Russell-Sluchansky wrote, "State judicial elections typically garner little attention, but Pennsylvania’s 2025 state Supreme Court races are shaping up to be the next major political battleground."[\[1\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-1) The state court had a 5-2 Democratic majority.[\[2\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-2) At the time of the election, the court had been controlled by Democrats since [2015](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2015 "Pennsylvania Supreme Court elections, 2015"), when Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht won election to their seats.[\[3\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-3) Pennsylvania used [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") to select a justice for an initial 10-year term, and used a [retention election](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to determine whether to keep them. If a justice was retained, they would serve another 10-year term. At the time of the election, Pennsylvania was one of eight states to use [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") for the initial selection of a justice and one of 22 to use [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") for the renewal of a term. According to Pennsylvania's Code of Judicial Conduct, justices were limited in their ability to campaign.[\[4\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-4) Both the Democratic and Republican parties said they would be involved in this race. The [Republican State Leadership Committee](https://ballotpedia.org/Republican_State_Leadership_Committee "Republican State Leadership Committee") ran ads on social media asking voters to vote against retaining the justices, which said, "In 2024, we voted by mail and flipped Pennsylvania red. This year, radical liberal judges are trying to secure another decade of power. We need you to stop them, show up again, vote 'no' in November."[\[5\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-5) The [Democratic National Committee](https://ballotpedia.org/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") announced on September 25 that they would invest six figures in the final weeks of the race, and Democratic politicians including Gov. [Josh Shapiro](https://ballotpedia.org/Josh_Shapiro "Josh Shapiro") (D), Sen. [Elissa Slotkin](https://ballotpedia.org/Elissa_Slotkin "Elissa Slotkin") (D-Mich.), and Rep. [Chris Deluzio](https://ballotpedia.org/Chris_Deluzio "Chris Deluzio") (D) campaigned in favor of retention.[\[6\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-7) Since retention elections were established in 1968, only one Pennsylvania justice, Russell Nigro (D) in 2005, was not retained.[\[8\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-8) Since 2020, in 102 elections, 100 justices (**98%**) won retention. The most recent justice in the U.S. to not win retention was [Yvonne Kauger](https://ballotpedia.org/Yvonne_Kauger "Yvonne Kauger") in Oklahoma in [2024](https://ballotpedia.org/Oklahoma_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024 "Oklahoma Supreme Court elections, 2024"). Candidates and results ---------------------- ### Donohue's seat [Christine Donohue](https://ballotpedia.org/Christine_Donohue) was retained to the _Pennsylvania Supreme Court_ on [November 4, 2025](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025) with 64.8% of the vote.

Selection --------- The **seven justices** of the [Pennsylvania Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court "Pennsylvania Supreme Court") are selected in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections").[\[16\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16) Justices serve 10-year terms, after which they must run in yes-no [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_elections "Retention elections") if they wish to remain on the court. A separate part of the ballot is designated for these elections, and justices' names appear without respect to party affiliation.[\[16\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)[\[17\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-retention-17) To learn more about these elections, visit the [Pennsylvania judicial elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_judicial_elections "Pennsylvania judicial elections") page. ### Qualifications To serve on the supreme court, a justice must: * have state residence for at least one year; * be a member of the state bar; and * be under the age of 75.[\[16\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)[\[18\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-new75-18) ### Chief justice The [Pennsylvania Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court "Pennsylvania Supreme Court") chooses its chief justice by seniority; the title is held by the longest-serving justice on the court.[\[16\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16)[\[19\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-code-19) ### Vacancies _See also: [How vacancies are filled in state supreme courts](https://ballotpedia.org/How_vacancies_are_filled_in_state_supreme_courts "How vacancies are filled in state supreme courts")_ In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [governor appoints a successor](https://ballotpedia.org/Gubernatorial_appointment_of_judges "Gubernatorial appointment of judges") who must be approved by a two-thirds vote of the [Pennsylvania Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Senate "Pennsylvania Senate"). Interim justices stand for election at the next municipal election occurring more than 10 months after the vacancy occurred.[\[16\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16) By tradition, appointed interim judges of the supreme court, superior court, or court of appeals do not go on to run for permanent seats. In other words, the governor appoints these judges with the expectation that the judge will only fill the interim vacancy.[\[16\]](https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025#cite_note-PAgeneral-16) The map below highlights how vacancies are filled in state supreme courts across the country. 2025 battleground elections --------------------------- _See also: [Battlegrounds](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia:Battlegrounds "Ballotpedia:Battlegrounds")_ This was a [battleground election](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia:Battlegrounds "Ballotpedia:Battlegrounds"). Pennsylvania retains Supreme Court justices, extending a Democratic majority on its highest court
=================================================================================================

90.5 WESA | By [Chris Potter](https://www.wesa.fm/people/chris-potter),

[Tom Riese](https://www.wesa.fm/people/tom-riese)

Published November 4, 2025 at 8:02 PM EST

Updated November 5, 2025 at 10:19 AM EST

*   [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=935012573999863&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wesa.fm%2Fpolitics-government%2F2025-11-04%2Fpa-supreme-court-retention-election-results)

    ![Image 4: Two white men and one white woman, all wearing suits, sit in chairs on a stage.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2b80e8e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1620x1080+0+0/resize/880x587!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fd7%2Ff8%2F6af062d142c4b7ab1ee57dd97289%2Fretention-1620x1080.jpg)

Jaxon White

/

WITF

From left to right, Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justices David Wecht, Christine Donohue and Kevin Dougherty sit at a forum held at Central High School in northern Philadelphia on Sept. 8, 2025.

Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty and David Wecht — all Democrats — will retain their seats on the state’s high court. The Associated Press called all three races just before 10 p.m. Tuesday night.

"I think the people of Pennsylvania understand that they have a well-functioning Supreme Court," Wecht told WESA just as the race was called. Recalling that the court had been rocked by a number of scandals in the years prior to the three justices' elections in 2015, he said, "We took a court that was to some extent deeply dysfunctional and in a state of turmoil, and with the cooperation of our colleagues \[we\] turned that court around."

"Despite the partisan attacks, tonight’s result confirms that Pennsylvanians have trust in the independence of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court and, additionally, appreciate the importance of a stable Pennsylvania Supreme Court," said Donohue in a statement from her campaign.

In a statement, Gov. Josh Shapiro praised voters who "sent a resounding message" by retaining the justices, saying they "will continue to defend the rule of law, safeguard our elections, and protect our constitutional rights.

"Here in the birthplace of democracy, the good people of Pennsylvania will always stand for freedom," the governor said.

The questions on the Nov. 4 ballot were simple, so simple that in most other years voters hardly give them a thought: Should the three justices be retained for an additional term as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania?

But by the time voters went to the polls Tuesday, they’d been [exposed to at least $9.5 million of in advertising](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/buying-time-2025-pennsylvania), according to a Brennan Center analysis, from independent good-government groups and national political parties alike. And whatever voters’ judgments on the three justices, the debate leading up to Election Day dealt a blow to the idea that retention votes are nonpartisan affairs.

“It's devolved into just another contested election,” [lamented Wecht in a WESA interview last month](https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2025-10-29/wecht-pa-supreme-court-retention-vote).

Leading into 2025, only one justice has ever _not_ been retained: Justice Russell Nigro was [ousted in 2005](https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2025-10-20/pa-supreme-court-wecht-retention) after voters responded to a controversial pay-raise scandal in Harrisburg.

But the three justices on the ballot for retention this fall were all elected as Democrats in 2015, and they have formed the core of the current five-member liberal court majority.

And while all three were recommended for retention by the state Bar Association, the world in which judges could count on coasting through retention votes appears to be over, said Chris Borick, who conducts polls and works as a professor of political science at Allentown’s Muhlenberg College.

"We are in a hyper-polarized era. It keeps rising everywhere, and it's certainly crept into how we think about the courts,” he said. “We see it in our polling on the \[U.S.\] Supreme Court, and it isn't much of a cognitive leap to go from a partisan election to a partisan retention race. Especially when there are these ad campaign to make us think that way.

This year, national groups and leaders — including [former President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump](https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2025-11-03/pa-supreme-court-retention-trump) — weighed in on the race. And both sides weighed in on weeks’ worth of mailers and advertising.

Conservatives targeted the justices for supporting pandemic-era business shutdowns, voting to change the state’s congressional map, and freeing accused sex offender Bill Cosby from jail. Some appeals stressed the idea that retention was a form of “term limit” — a concept polls show is broadly popular, especially when distrust of elected officials is high.

Supporters, including Shapiro, have stressed that the justices will protect abortion access and would serve as a bulwark at a time when “threats to our freedoms are very real,” as Shapiro said in an ad recorded to support retention.

With help from labor groups and trial lawyers, Democrats appear to have outgunned conservatives in campaign spending, despite early warnings that the well-heeled billionaires such as Pennsylvania hedge-fund manager Jeffrey Yass might seek to “buy” the ouster of the justices. And Democratic party leaders were more visible in other ways, with Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin [making multiple visits to the state](https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2025-10-17/pa-supreme-court-ken-martin) on behalf of the justices.

DNC officials said the party invested sums in the low six digits to help the state party organize volunteers and other get-out-the-vote efforts. The party said its phone-bank effort made 133,000 calls to voters in the waning days of the campaign.

Borick said retention supporters have “outspent the ‘no’ side considerably” — two pro-retention ads aired in the space of three minutes on the TV he had on in the background while he was on the phone with WESA. And he said after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the constitutional right to an abortion, “reproductive rights is still fresh on people’s minds. That’s made it pretty potent, and it’s been front and center in almost every ad.”

Still, he said the anti-retention side was shrewd in its messaging as well. Urging voters to think about a “no” vote as a form of term limit made a lot of sense, he said. “We aren’t happy with political institutions in this country right now,” he said. And term limits “almost always poll pretty well.”

Voters often rely on party affiliation to decide who to support, he said, but in a retention race — where no party labels are given to the judges — “you go to other cues.” And this year, he said, “I think it comes down to a broader feeling about the institutions and the system. That probably helps the 'no' vote.”

But in the end, the justices may have been helped by outside factors, including a desire on the part of Democratic voters to brush back Trump. But Wecht himself told WESA that "I'm sure there are many macro and micro forces that played a role, but i'll leave it to the pubndits to speculate on that." For his part, he said, the important thing was that "Every Pennsylvanian is entitled to a court that focuses on quality jurisprudence, instead of nonsense. And that's what they get."

There were concerns that rejecting the justices would have proven hugely disruptive to Pennslyvania's legal system.

When voters reject a judge who is up for retention, it leaves that seat on the bench vacant until voters choose a new one in the next off-year election — unless the governor and the Republican-led Senate cannot agree on a replacement.

Observers say that given the partisan divides evident in the retention fight itself, [making an interim selection would not be easy](https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2025-10-20/pa-supreme-court-wecht-retention). The defeat of all three justices would mean a four-member court, one evenly divided between justices who ran as Democrats and those who ran as Republicans, for up to two years.

**Statewide Appellate Courts**

The Supreme Court justices were not the only statewide jurists facing a retention vote.

Commonwealth Court Judge [Michael Wojcik](https://www.pacourts.us/courts/commonwealth-court-judges/judge-michael-h-wojcik), a former solicitor for Allegheny County elected in 2015 as a Democrat, is seeking to return to the nine-member bench, which hears cases involving governmental agencies and policies.

Alice Beck Dubow, another Democrat from the class of 2015, similarly seeks to be returned to the Superior Court, which hears appeals from Common Pleas Courts in civil and criminal matters.

Each of the statewide courts also featured a more conventional contest for a vacant seat. Republican Matt Wolford and Democrat Stella Tsai were seeking the Commonwealth Court seat left vacant by the retirement of Ellen Ceisler. Both candidates come “highly recommended” by the Pennsylvania Bar Association.

The court’s makeup currently includes five members elected as Republicans and three elected as Democrats.

Tsai has served as a Philadelphia Common Pleas Court judge since 2016, presiding over cases regarding election candidacy challenges, guardianship, medical malpractice and disputes over estates.

Wolford has long represented clients before Commonwealth Court. The Erie County attorney has had his own practice since 1999, but previously worked at the state Attorney General’s Office and the state Department of Environmental Protection.

Three candidates are running to join the 15-member the state Superior Court, whose ranks currently include eight judges who ran as Democrats and six who ran as Republicans.

Republican Maria Battista, Democrat Brandon Neuman and the Liberal Party’s Daniel Wassmer all bring unique backgrounds to the race.

Battista is a legal consultant who long worked in private practice and was an attorney with the state Office of General Counsel.

Neuman is a Washington County Common Pleas judge, and a former state House member.

Wassmer, an attorney and instructor, has run for several offices for the Liberal Party (formerly the Keystone Party), including state Attorney General and U.S. Senate.

The candidates, like those running for Commonwealth Court, are also vying for a $247,188 annual salary.
